stem: Applying the principles of EBM, which of the following must be considered when choosing a new drug for treating a patient?
options: Number of patients to be treated in order to achieve a single case of success
The validity of the evidence for the treatment
All of the other 4 listed options
the generalisability of trial results to your clinical sample
The expected rate of spontaneous resolution in your clinical sample
correctAnswer: All of the other 4 listed options 
explanation: Applying principles of EBM, one must check for the internal validity of a study and the degree of generalisability before adapting results to clinical practice. One must also be aware of the fact that though clinically more meaningful, NNTs quoted in RCTs may not translate to the same extent in actual clinical practice. One way of appreciating the usefulness of a newly introduced drug is to calculate the NNT for one 's own clinical population (target population). To enable this one may estimate patient expected event rate (PEER) which is given by expected spontaneous resolution rate or the response rate for an existing standard treatment.

stem: As a part of National confi dential Inquiry on Suicides and Homicides in people with mental illness, data was collected to study the association of dementia and suicides (Purandare, N., et al (2009). Suicide in dementia: 9-year national clinical survey in England and Wales. The British Journal of Psychiatry, 194(2), 175-180.) All suicides registered by the Offi ce for National Statistics from 1 April 1996 until 31 December 2004 were considered.When NHS records showed that contact had occurred in the 12 months before the suicide, the person became an `Inquiry case'. For each Inquiry case, the consultant psychiatrist was sent a questionnaire and asked to complete it based on their knowledge of the patient, psychiatry case notes, and in discussion with other members of the mental health team. The clinicians were asked for an ICD-10 primary diagnosis and a total of 118 patients with dementia were identifi ed. For each individual with dementia, four gender-matched suicide cases of patients without a diagnosis of dementia (controls) nearest in age to the dementia patients (n=472) were extracted from the database. This selection was masked and the researchers were unaware of the behavioural and clinical characteristics of controls. All controls were individually matched for gender and 462/472 (98%) for age within 2 years of the index case (3-year diff erence for seven cases, 5-year diff erence for two cases and 6-year diff erence for one case). Over the 9-year study period, the Inquiry received notifi cations of 45 012 deaths by suicide. Of these, 11 733 (26.1%) were confi rmed to have been in contact with mental health services in the year prior to death. Completed questionnaires were received for 11 512 cases, a response rate of 98.1%. In 11 141 cases (97.9% of the 11 375 cases that included data on primary diagnosis), a psychiatric diagnosis was recorded. In 118 (1.1%) of these cases, the individuals had received a clinical diagnosis of dementia from their psychiatrist . Please see the attached table. Weaknesses of this study include which of the following? 
options: Low number of cases compared to controls in the sample
Statistical power of the study is limited
ndings to all patients with dementia
correctAnswer: Limited generalisability offi ndings to all patients with dementia 
explanation:


Follow up method has not been used for the study. Deliberately more controls have been chosen than cases to make the study more powerful. Hence having low number of cases compared to controls is not a weakness. The research question asked here can be ethically answered only through a retrospective design. The generalisability of the study is limited to patients with dementia who are in contact with the mental health services in the 12 months preceding their suicide. We cannot generalize thesefi ndings to dementia patients who have never contacted the services, who had no contact in the preceding 12 months and those who were managed by primary care throughout their illness.

stem: A multicentre trial to assess eff ectiveness of CBT-based treatment in early intervention for psychosisfi nds a signifi cant eff ect in favour of the intervention. But secondary analysis reveals signifi cant trial centre-eff ect on the outcome. Which of the following could possibly explain such an eff ect?
explanation: Confounding by cluster refers to false eff ects in trials where subjects response is based on cluster membership rather than an individual treatment eff ect. This is often seen in educational interventions in GP practices where a residential area or neighbourhood socioeconomic status may cluster individuals in one practice who may markedly diff er from those in other GP practices. It is also noted in psychological interventions where therapist eff ect tends to cluster the subjects diff erently. Another example is multicentred trials where the centre eff ect may be prominent when there are diff erences in organisation, delivery and personnel from centre to centre.

stem: A randomized trial of oral antiretroviral therapy was conducted to evaluate the use of antiretroviral treatment as preexposure prophylaxis among HIV-1 –serodiscordant heterosexual couples from Kenya and Uganda. The HIV-1 –seronegative partner in each couple was randomly assigned to one of three study regimens — once-daily tenofovir (TDF), combination tenofovir – emtricitabine (TDF –FTC), or matching placebo — and followed monthly for up to 36 months. Of the enrolled 4758 couples 4747 were followed: 1584 randomly assigned to TDF, 1579 to TDF –FTC, and 1584 to placebo. A total of 82 HIV-1 infections occurred in seronegative participants during the study, 17 in the TDF group, 13 in the TDF –FTC group and 52 in the placebo group, indicating a relative reduction of 67% in the incidence of HIV-1 with TDF (95% confi dence interval [CI], 44 to 81; P<0.001) and of 75% with TDF –FTC (95% CI, 55 to 87; P<0.001). Protective eff ects of TDF –FTC and TDF alone against HIV-1 were not signifi cantly diff erent (P=0.23), and both study medications signifi cantly reduced the HIV-1 incidence among both men and women. Eight participants receiving active treatment were found to have been infected with HIV-1 at baseline, and among these, antiretroviral resistance developed in two during the study. An estimate of the primary endpoint in the modifi ed Intention-to-Treat Analysis is shown in a graph below. At 36 months after the randomisation, the probability for the partners to remain seronegative despite receiving placebo is 

explanation: The classical triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion is rarely present in Wernicke's encephalopathy. The syndrome is much more common than is widely believed. A presumptive diagnosis of Wernicke's encephalopathy should, therefore, be made in any patient undergoing detoxifi cation who experiences any of the following signs; Ataxia, Hypothermia and hypotension, Confusion, ophthalmoplegia/ Nystagmus, Memory disturbance and coma/unconsciousness.

stem: A 64-year-old lady is having problems with alcohol use for many years now. She presents with back pain, nocturia and tiredness. Which of the following electrolyte disturbance is likely?
explanation: Chronic alcoholism is a predisposing factor for hypocalcemia and is associated with chronic pancreatitis.

stem: Which of the following potentially dangerous side eff ect is associated with clonidine, when used for treating opioid dependence?
explanation: Clonidine is not so popular now due to high rates of hypotension associated with it. If the short duration of Opioid withdrawal treatment is desirable, a2 adrenergic agonists (e.g. clonidine and Lofexidine) are preferable to methadone. As Lofexidine do not control symptoms such as nausea, additional symptom support using metoclopramide, antidiarrhoeals etc. may be required.

stem: Which of the following cognitions describe abstinence violation eff ect in those with alcohol dependence?
options: I will drink just once; this won't harm me
I had a drink; so I have turned into a drinker again
It is not up to me to change myself
correctAnswer: I had a drink; so I have turned into a drinker again 
explanation: Abstinence violation eff ect refers to the cognition that "I had a drink; so I am a drinker again'. This may force patients to reinstate full pattern of drinking.

stem: Tolerance is least likely to develop for which of the following symptoms of amphetamine use?
explanation: Regular use of amphetamines induces tolerance to some eff ects, which means that more and more of the drug is required to produce the desired eff ects. Tolerance does not develop to all eff ects at the same rate, for example to the vasopressor actions.

stem: A chronic alcohol abuser presented to A&E with history suggestive of memory impairment and gait disturbance. On examination he has a malnourished appearance with scaly skin lesions. Which of the following is recommended before discharge?
explanation: Treatment with intravenous thiamine (B1) is recommended for patients at high risk of Wernicke- Korsakoff syndrome. (Pabrinex(r) IVHP 5mL ampoules three times daily for two days). Following the initial IV loading dose, oral supplementation should include thiamine 100mg three times daily. If the patient is at risk of malnutrition then oral thiamine 100mg three times daily should continue indefi nitely. There is little evidence to substantiate the use of Vitamin B Compound Strong tablets.

stem: The lifetime prevalence of OCD in the general population is
explanation: A national, community-based survey of OCD in the UK (1993, 10,000 people) found that 1.0% of men and 1.5% of women reported symptoms in the previous month. A survey of a random sample of people living in private households in the UK (2000, 8580 adults aged 16- 74 years) found that 1.1% of those surveyed reported symptoms of OCD during the previous week. ECA, the epidemiological catchment area survey carried out in the USA in 1984 (about 10,000 people) found an age- and sex-standardised annual prevalence of OCD in people aged 26 to 64 years of 1.3%, and a lifetime prevalence of 2.3%. Thus, between 2-3% of general population has 'lifetime' history of OCD. The rates may be higher in children considered alone.

stem: What percentage of patients on clozapine develop agranulocytosis?
explanation: It is 0.7%. The risk of Agranulocytosis decreases to 0.07% after thefi rst year of treatment. Risk factor includes increasing age and Asian race. In contrast, the risk of the more benign neutropenia is higher, estimated to be 1-2%.

stem: The mean age of onset of chronic fatigue syndrome is between
explanation: The prevalence of Chronic Fatigue Syndrome is nearly 0.5% with a higher rate in women [M-F - 1:3], those belonging to lower occupational status and educational background. The mean age of onset is between 29-35 years. Mean illness duration is 3-9 years. The prevalence seems to be lower among children and adolescents.

stem: A middle-aged woman who was taking lithium presents with weight gain and constipation along with lethargy. What proportion of those who take lithium develop hypothyroidism?
explanation: The prevalence of clinical hypothyroidism during lithium treatment varies between 5 to 10%. The main risk factor is female gender (women 14% v. men 4.5%). Women were at highest risk during thefi rst two years of lithium treatment, and women starting lithium aged 40-59 years had the greatest prevalence (> 20%). [The British Journal of Psychiatry (1999) 175: 336-339]

stem: Which of the following statement regarding rating scales for depression is true?
options: Zung depression scale is observer rated
Geriatric depression scale has more somatic than cognitive items of depression
The maximum score for Hamilton depression scale (17 items) is 52
Beck's depression scale is more sensitive to change than other scales
correctAnswer: The maximum score for Hamilton depression scale (17 items) is 52 
explanation: Zung rating scale is self-rated. Beck's has 21 items. MADRS is the most sensitive to change among commonly used depression scales.

stem: The prevalence of psychotic illness in patients with epilepsy is;
explanation: The prevalence of psychotic illness in patients with epilepsy is at least 4%. A diagnosis of temporal lobe epilepsy does not seem to confer additional risk.

stem: Which of the following signs is not present in Wernicke's encephalopathy?
explanation: Wernicke's encephalopathy is an acute condition characterized by well-known triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and global confusional state. Classic triad of confusion, ataxia and nystagmus is only present in 10% of patients and 80% of patients are not diagnosed before post mortem. These eye signs are usually bilateral but not necessarily symmetrical. WE is directly caused by acute thiamine defi ciency, due to inadequate dietary intake, reduced gastrointestinal absorption, decreased hepatic storage, and impaired utilization. Peripheral neuropathy, a sign of beri-beri, results from more chronic vitamin defi ciency states.

stem: Compared to the general population, patients with schizophrenia are less likely to die from
explanation: The relationship between cancer and schizophrenia is not straightforward and can appear paradoxical. For example, tobacco smoking rates in those with schizophrenia are typically twice those of the background population which would suggest higher rates of lung cancer in those with schizophrenia, but some studies quote a lower incidence of lung cancer in people with schizophrenia (Hippisley-Cox et al 2007). The excess mortality in schizophrenia is attributable to cardiovascular, neoplastic and respiratory disease (Leucht et al 2007). People with schizophrenia are more likely to die prematurely than the general population from both suicide and physical ill health. (Ref: Cancer and schizophrenia: is there a paradox?- Richard Hodgson, Wildgust & Bushe)

stem: A man with schizophrenia is on clozapine but is still experiencing active psychotic symptoms. The best drug for augmentation is
explanation: Clozapine is a polyvalent drug with a comparatively weak dopamine receptor blockade. Therefore, the combined use of substituted benzamides such as sulpride or Amisulpride that have highly selective dopamine receptor blockade is, in particular, a preferred strategy (Kerwin, 2005)

stem: The standardized mortality rate for major depression is
explanation: The SMR for major depression is 20 times that expected; The mortality rate for manic depression is 15 times higher than the expected (Harris and Barraclough 1997)

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the longevity of patients with schizophrenia is based on epidemiological evidence?
options: Most common cause of death is suicide
The mortality rate is climbing down in the last two decades
All patients who die prematurely have a diagnosis of metabolic syndrome
Have higher mortality risk than those with bipolar disorder
Have 2.6 times higher mortality than general population
correctAnswer: Have 2.6 times higher mortality than general population 
explanation: The SMR is 2.6 for both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and it is showing a worryingly increasing trend. Gelder et al. (2005) Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edition pg 294

stem: Mr Y was admitted to a neuro-rehabilitation unit for the treatment of brain injury. He was reported to present with spontaneous, unprovoked crying although he is not depressed. You are requested to review and advise treatment. The drug of choice is;
explanation: This patient is suff ering from Pathological laughing and crying syndrome, also called emotional incontinence/emotionalism/pseudobulbar aff ect. This refers to spontaneous, unprovoked laughter or crying seen in patients with brain damage; it occurs in response to non-specifi c stimuli, in the absence of associated mood change (mood incongruent aff ect) and the absence of voluntary control of facial expression. The aff ect change is generally transient but distressing due to perceived loss of control. In a study, 66% of people with MS and pathological laughing/crying responded to 75 mg of amitriptyline per day. Improvement in symptoms also occurs with either amantadine or levodopa administration. Fluoxetine and sertraline have been evaluated in small parallel RCTs with favourable results; citalopram in a cross over trial showed signifi cant benefi ts and fewer side-eff ects.

stem: Which is the most reliable risk factor for completed suicide?
explanation: The strongest risk factor of suicide is DSH history with previous suicide attempts

stem: The risk of completed suicide in patients with history of deliberate self-harm is
explanation: The strongest risk factor of suicide is history of deliberate self harm. Prognosis of non-fatal DSH: 20% repeat and 1% die in next year. 10% eventually complete suicide. The risk of suicide within one year of DSH is 0.7% (nearly 1 in 100); more in males 1.1%; 0.5% in females. This is 66 x the general population risk.(Ref: Emergencies in psychiatry-119)

stem: Which of the following psychometric tests exploit the personality dynamics that are outside the conscious awareness of the tested subject?
explanation: Thematic Apperception Test is a projective test.

stem: A young man is living with his family. He reports being interested in becoming super-fi t. He does a lot of exercises, and His mother has complained of behaviour change recently. His sleep is disturbed and is crying for no reason. He was observed to laugh inappropriately. The diagnosis is;
explanation: This man is presenting with features of steroid-induced psychosis, due to abuse of anabolic steroids. Athletes and body builders often tend to use anabolic steroids. They produce euphoriant eff ects, increased muscle mass, muscle strength and a sense of increased energy levels. It is associated with mental health problems such as psychosis, emotional instability, increased aggressiveness, persecutory/grandiose ideas, depressive illness and chronic fatigue. Psychotic symptoms are often associated, up to half the cases. (Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry- 547)

stem: Most cases of postpartum psychosis develop in which of the following postpartum periods?
explanation: Postpartum psychosis occurs in 1 –2/1000 childbearing women within thefi rst two weeks after delivery. In some patients, as early as 2 –3 days after childbirth, paranoid, grandiose, or bizarre delusions, mood swings, confused thinking, and grossly disorganized behavior that represent a dramatic change from previous functioning may be seen. It is far less common than postpartum depression which aff ects 10% – 13% of new mothers, and the maternity blues, which aff ects 50% –75% of postpartum women. http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3109493/

stem: Which of the following rating scales employ Life Change Units?
explanation: To measure stress according to the Holmes and Rahe Social Readjustment Scale, the number of "Life Change Units" that apply to events in the past year of an individual's life is employed.

stem: Number of people suff ering from mixed anxiety and depressive symptoms at any given time in UK is
explanation: According to some studies, mixed anxiety and depression is one of the most common mental disorder in Britain with nearly 9% of people meeting criteria for diagnosis - The Offi ce for National Statistics Psychiatric Morbidity report (2001). "Mixed anxiety and depressive symptoms that do not reach thresholds for formal psychiatric diagnosis make up nearly half of all psychological problems in the UK and are nearly four times more common than depressive disorder alone". Walters, K., Buszewicz, M., Weich, S., & King, M. (2011). Mixed anxiety and depressive disorder outcomes: prospective cohort study in primary care. The British Journal of Psychiatry, 198(6), 472-478.

stem: Which of the following psychiatric disorder is projected to become the second largest cause of disease burden worldwide by 2020?
explanation: Unipolar depression will rank second while bipolar disorder in sixth place when global disease burden are considered in 2020, according to current projections.

stem: The prevalence of epilepsy in patients with schizophreniform psychosis is:
explanation: The point prevalence is between 0.4-1%.

stem: Which of the following is true about the trend shown by the epidemiology of depression?
options: Point prevalence is steady across years
Detection of depression is not infl
Middle aged men are increasingly having more depression
Highest risk for depression is in those over age 30 yrs
explanation: Various studies including NCS and its replication NCS-R, NSEARC and ECA have implicated that lifetime prevalence of depression is increasing.

stem: The prevalence of depression in patients with Coronary Heart Disease is
explanation: The prevalence rate of clinically signifi cant depression among patients with coronary heart disease is approximately 21.5%. The risk of clinical depression in patients with CHD is 2-3 times the rate of the general population.

stem: Which of the following statements about Y-BOCS (Yale-Brown obsessive compulsive scale) is not true?
options: Rating is on a 4 point scale
explanation: Y-BOCS does not rate obsessive personality traits. The Y-BOCS is a clinician administered semi-structured interview that rates obsessions and compulsions separately on time occupied, distress, impairment, resistance, and control. It is now considered as the scale of choice for rating OCD symptoms.

stem: The Yale-Brown obsessive-compulsive scale covers all of the following aspects except
explanation: YBOCS, the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale, is the preferred measurement tool for measuring the severity and nature of OCD symptoms. It does not measure anankastic traits.

stem: Which of the following drugs is contraindicated in renal failure?
explanation: Amisulpride is renally excreted almost exclusively. Hence renal failure will be a contraindication to use this drug.

stem: According to CATIE study of patients with Schizophrenia, the number of patients meeting criteria for metabolic syndrome, ranges between what percentages;
explanation: The prevalence of metabolic syndrome was 40.9% to 42.7% according to two diff erent criteria used for the diagnosis of metabolic syndrome in the CATIE sample. Interestingly, the prevalence was higher in women 54.2% than in men (36.0%).

stem: Which of the following may help diff erentiating borderline personality from bipolar disorder?
options: Impulsivity in bipolar disorder is chronic rather than episodic
Mood changes lasts for many days in borderline personality
Emptiness is often used as the mood descriptor in borderline personality
Elated mood shifts are often seen in borderline personality
correctAnswer: Emptiness is often used as the mood descriptor in borderline personality 
explanation: In Bipolar Disorder the onset is in early 20s (later than borderline), mood changes are observable spontaneoulsy rather than being precipitated solely by external events, if present, episodic self harm attempts are usually related to depression, though self mutilation is rare. Patients with borderline PD use 'emptiness' as a descriptor for their mood more often than those with bipolar disorder.

stem: Which of the following is correct with respect to automatism?
options: Sane automatism is due to internal causes
Automatism is commonly seen in REM sleep behavioural disorder
Subjects cannot have complete acquittal when making a plea of automatism
correctAnswer: Epileptic automatism is classifi ed as insane automatism 
explanation: Automatism is not a common plea. Insane automatism is due to internal causes such as epilepsy - these are seen as irreversible and may lead to psychiatric disposal if required. Sane automatisms can lead to complete acquittal if internal factors are ruled out - i.e. recurrence risk is low. In REM sleep behavioural disordered, organised actions leading to automatisms are extremely rare.

stem: Miss. Y is a 24-year-old woman recently diagnosed with debilitating symptoms of premenstrual syndrome. She asks for a prescription offl uoxetine. Which of the following is an accurate statement in this context?
options: Fluoxetine provides relief only after continuous use for at least 5 cycles of menstruation
Fluoxetinehas no evidence in treating premenstrual syndrome
Fluoxetine provides relief in premenstrual syndrome irrespective of its eff
Fluoxetine provides relief in premenstrual syndrome through its antidepressant activity
Fluoxetine is the only antidepressant that has been studied for use in premenstrual dyndrome
correctAnswer: Fluoxetine provides relief in premenstrual syndrome irrespective of its eff ect on depressive features 
explanation: In severe premenstrual syndrome, the response rate for SSRIs is 60-90% compared to 30-40% for placebo. The eff ective medications include both SSRIs and the SNRI Venlafaxine. The two most studied SSRIs arefl uoxetine and sertraline. The most eff ective drug is Fluoxetine; it shows response within one menstrual cycle which is too rapid to be a true antidepressant eff ect.

stem: Which of the following substance is implicated in epilepsy-related depression seen in patients treated with certain anticonvulsants?
explanation: Folate defi ciency may be a cause of depression in psychiatric patients. Patients with epilepsy have a lower folate serum level than control subjects. The reduction in serum folate is associated with the induction of enzymes by antiepileptic drugs.

stem: Mr. X suff ers from sweating, fatigue, heat intolerance, weight loss, weakness,fi ne tremor, and tachycardia. What is the most commonly seen psychiatric diagnosis associated with this condition?
explanation: Hyperthyroidism can cause many of the same symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder and must be ruled out

stem: Which of the following can increase the likelihood of neurotoxicity when prescribed with lithium?
explanation: Lithium and haloperidol form a useful combo and is widely used. But reports of neurotoxicity suggest that if lithium is in higher end of serum range with high dose of haloperidol use, delirium and other acute neurotoxic eff ects could emerge. (See Maudsley guidelines 2006 page 114)

stem: Dysthymia is seen in what proportion of the general population?
explanation: The lifetime prevalence of dysthymia in the general population is approximately 5%. (M: F=1:2)

stem: A 43-year-old woman works as a medical secretary. She is having signifi cant problems with personal debts and believes that with oncoming global economic recession she will go bankrupt and may end up 'living on charity'. Which of the following cognitive distortion is she having?
explanation: In catastrophic thinking, subjects predict the worst possible catastrophic outcome from a process despite having equal or better probabilities of other diff erent outcomes.

stem: CBT is contraindicated in
explanation: In severe dementia, cognitive approaches are not useful and must be avoided if possible in those who are prone to catastrophic reactions.

stem: A child is abused by her step-father. You want tofi nd out if her sibling has a similar risk. What is the best way to deal with this?
options: Family therapy with the abuser as well present
explanation: A single session with the child would provide a platform for exploration of risk, which would then inform whether psychotherapy is necessary/warranted. You wouldn't set up psychotherapy straight away without knowing if it were indicated.

stem: Social phobia is most likely to be associated with which of the following?
explanation: Social phobia is characterised by severe anxiety restricted to a particular social situation, leading to avoidance that social situation. This anxiety is not secondary to delusional or obsessive thoughts.

stem: A 77-year-old man comes to A&E with agitation and confusion. What is the most appropriate drug to prescribe?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis in this situation is Delirium. In terms of pharmacological management, oral antipsychotic medication should be triedfi rst. They are the main stay of treatment, eff ective in all types of delirium and are helpful in controlling agitation and aggressive behaviour. Oral haloperidol is the drug of choice and has been found to be eff ective in some RCTs. The usual dose recommended for the elderly is 0.5-1 mg BD. (Ref: Oxford Handbook of Old Age Psychiatry-pg92)

stem: A 75-year-old man is taking Aspirin and Selegiline for his movement disorder. He is unable to work due to problems with his memory. The correct drug of choice in his treatment is;
explanation: This man is probably suff ering from Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD). Rivastigmine has been evaluated in the symptomatic treatment of patients with mild-to-moderate dementia associated with idiopathic Parkinson's disease. The mode of administration could be oral or a transdermal patch. Although the evidence is preliminary, it is the best available evidence among the other options for Parkinson's related dementia. Rivastigmine appears to improve both cognition and activities of daily living in patients with PDD, resulting in a clinically meaningful benefi t in a large number of cases. (Ref: Emre M, Aarsland D, Albanese A et al. Rivastigmine for dementia associated with Parkinson's disease. N Engl J Med 2004;351:2509-2518)

stem: A 70-year-old man who was previouslyfi t and well has reported that three months ago when he was in a supermarket, he started crying uncontrollably for no reason. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This person is exhibiting pseudobulbar aff ect, which is also called emotional incontinence or emotional lability. It is most commonly observed in people with traumatic brain injury, stroke, Parkinson's disease and dementia including Alzheimer's disease.

stem: A 65-year-old woman has a history of cognitive impairment and behavioural disturbance for more than a year. She has hypertension, diabetes and hypercholesterolemia. MMSE score is 19/30. CT brain scan shows multiple white matter hyperintensities. The most important initial treatment is
explanation: The diagnosis is vascular dementia. The management options are currently very limited and focus on controlling the underlying risk factors for cerebrovascular disease. Daily aspirin may delay the course of the disease. None of the currently available drugs is licensed for vascular dementia in the UK.

stem: The prevalence of paraphrenia in elderly above the age of 65 is
explanation: People with late paraphrenia represent approximately 10% of the elderly population of psychiatric hospitals. The reported prevalence of the disorder among the elderly living in the community ranges from 0.1 to 4%, and its incidence has been estimated to be between 10-26 per 100 000 per year. (Almeida, O. P., Howard, R., Forstl, H., et al. (1992) Late paraphrenia: a review. International Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, 7, 543-548.)

stem: Binge eating is seen in what proportion of patients with Alzheimer's disease?
explanation: Bulimic behaviour may be a result of improper brain functioning due to Alzheimer's. It is diffi cult to manage, as mostly the Alzheimer's brain is unable to process any instructions regarding the restrictions on eating and the person is unable to control binging and purging cycle. It is seen in 10% of patients with AD.

stem: Proportion of patients with variant for of CJD that present with cerebellar ataxia is given by
explanation: The early clinical presentation of vCJD resembles kuru and consists of behavioural and psychiatric disturbances, peripheral sensory disturbance and cerebellar ataxia. Common early psychiatric features include dysphoria, withdrawal, anxiety, insomnia, and apathy. Neurological symptoms have preceded psychiatric symptoms in 15% of cases studied, and are present in combination with psychiatric symptoms in 22% of cases from the onset of disease (Spencer et al., BMJ. 2002 Jun 22;324(7352):1479-82.). About 10% of vCJD cases present with cerebellar ataxia rather than cognitive impairment, so-called ataxic vCJD.(Wadsworth et al., 2003)

stem: In old age, what percentage of patients that commit suicide have seen their GP on the same day of their suicide?
explanation: The percentage of older patients who committed suicide that visited their primary care physician- 20% on the same day as their suicide, 40- 50% within 1 week and 70% within one month.

stem: The prevalence of Alzheimer's dementia in elderly above the age of 95 is
explanation: The prevalence of dementia increases exponentially with age. About one-third of the population aged 85 and over has dementia, with prevalence ranging from 0.4% under 60 years to 45% at 95 years and over.

stem: In patients older than 70 years of age, the rate of progression from Mild Cognitive Impairment to full-blown dementia in a year is
explanation: While the rate of progression to dementia is 1-2% for cognitively normal individuals aged 65 or older, the rates for all MCI entities are systematically higher and most studies report rate between 10 and 15 % per annum, generally over 5 year periods.

stem: A four-year-old boy who was born in India presents with epilepsy, severe mental retardation and behavioural problems. On examination, you note the lack of pigment in skin and hair. The diagnosis is
explanation: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive metabolic genetic disorder. A defect in Phenylalanine Hydroxylase (PAH) or cofactor (biopterin) with accumulation of phenylalanine. Symptoms absent neonatally, a later development of seizures (25% generalized). Clinical features include fair skin, blue eyes, blond hair, and recurrent rashes. Untreated infants have an unusual mouse-like body odour. Microcephaly is seen in 50% of cases. Without treatment mild to profound mental retardation, language delay, destructiveness, self-injury, hyperactivity could result. A low-phenylalanine diet must be usually continued throughout the childhood.

stem: A 7-year-old boy has a moderate degree of learning disability. He is socially disinhibited and excessively friendly. These are behavioural phenotypes of which of the following conditions?
explanation: Williams syndrome- is characterised by hypercalcemia (50% of cases) with supra valvular aortic stenosis and unusual facies. It is a rare condition. The majority of these subjects have a mild to moderate degree of mental retardation. Clinical features include short stature, growth retardation, unusual facial features including broad forehead, elfi n-like facies, hoarse voice, premature wrinkling and sagging of the skin, renal and cardiovascular abnormalities (supra valvular aortic stenosis); thyroid abnormalities; hypercalcemia. Behavioural phenotypes include: Anxiety, hypersensitivity or outgoing, sociable, disinhibited, excessive friendliness.

stem: The prevalence of schizophrenia in the learning disabled population is
explanation: Psychotic disorders, particularly schizophrenia, appear to be more common in those who also have a learning disability. The rate is raised threefold over the general population. Most studies report a prevalence of 3 to 3.5 percent for schizophrenia.

stem: Deletion of a segment of chromosome 15q or the segment being solely derived from maternal chromosome leads to
explanation: The genomic imprinting syndromes of Angelman and Prader-Willi can be inherited in two diff erent ways. The most common mechanism is a complete deletion of the segment (no gene copies left). The second mechanism is called uniparental disomy where the segments do not go missing, but instead, are derived solely from one parent. In the latter case, maternal inheritance of the segment (maternal UPD) leads to Prader-Willi while paternal UPD leads to Angelman's.

stem: The highest incidence of intellectual disabilities is seen in
explanation: The prevalence of intellectual disabilities at any one time is estimated to range from 1 percent to 3 percent of the population. The incidence of intellectual disabilities is diffi cult to calculate because mild intellectual disability sometimes goes unrecognised until middle childhood. The highest incidence is in school-age children, with the peak at ages 10 to 14 years. Intellectual disabilities are about 1.5 times more common among men than among women. Those with severe or profound disabilities have high mortality rates because of the complications of associated physical disorders.

stem: Lyonisation is a feature associated with which of the following disorders?
explanation: Whenever there are more than 1 (haploid) set of X-linked genes in a cell, all but one of the genes are inactivated at random and have no phenotypic expression. This process, called Lyonization, is inherently random explaining the more variability in the expression of certain X- linked disorders in women. In individuals with the Klinefelter (XXY) karyotype who are phenotypically male, Lyonization silences the extra set of X genes.

stem: All the following disorders have been found to be signifi cantly comorbid with pathological gambling except
explanation: Impulse control underlies the mechanism of pathological gambling. Hence, high degree of comorbid ADHD, substance use and other impulse control disorders are found. Depression is also highly correlated.

stem: A 24 years old male has repeated emotional outbursts and is impulsive. He has been arrested on numerous occasions for assaulting his partner. Most likely diagnosis is
explanation: This patient is exhibiting antisocial traits.

stem: The prevalence of psychosis in prison population is
explanation: The weighted prevalence of probable functional psychosis in the past year was 4.5 per thousand (95% CI=3.1 to 5.8) in the household survey. In the prison survey, the weighted prevalence was over ten times greater: 52 per thousand (95% CI=45 to 60). Apart from a minority of prisoners with symptoms attributable to psychoactive substances, the clinical symptom profi le of psychosis is the same in both settings. http://ajp.psychiatryonline.org/cgi/content/full/ajp;162/4/774.

stem: What percentage of people convicted of indecent exposure have no previous record of sexual off ences?
explanation: 20% arefi rst-time off enders and have no previous record of sexual off ences. 60% of them have a previous history of sexual off ences. 70% of them have a history of previous sexual and non-sexual off ences. Nearly 20-30% of them reoff end.

stem: You are asked to conclude whether automatism could be used as a defence. Which of the following statements is true?
options: Sane automatisms cannot lead to total acquittal
Sane automatisms are due to internal causes
In proven insane automatisms, the accused cannot be found guilty by reason of insanity
explanation: Automatism: It is a rare plea. Legal classifi cation includes sane automatism where the act is one off , often acquittal takes place. Hypoglycemia (isolated), night terror and dissociative states can be classed as sane automatisms. Here the cause is often 'external'. Insane automatisms are likely to recur ('internal') and the counsel can plead not guilty by reason of insanity (insanity defence). Night walking, epilepsy, hypoglycemia due to a recurring condition are classed under this. There is no medical sense in these classifi cations. Automatism is a plea by a criminally accused that his or her actions were not under the control of the conscious mind. In other words, claiming that one's bodily movements were not willfully executed and were involuntary.

stem: Low rates of recidivism in a sexual off ence are indicated by which of the following features?
correctAnswer: Incestual sex off ence against a child 
explanation: Rapists tend to be more criminally versatile than child molesters and are more likely to reoff end non-sexually than sexually. Among child molesters, the risk of sexual recidivism is higher for homosexual and extra-familial sex off enders than for heterosexual and incest off enders.

stem: In terms of off ending behaviour of adults with learning disabilities, which of the following statements is correct?
options: Adults with severe learning disabilities are likely to be convicted of murder
Adults with severe learning disabilities are likely to be foundfi
Fire setting is the most frequent off
ending is more frequent than physical aggression
Adults with borderline and mild learning disabilities account for most of the off

explanation: Individuals with mild learning disability show a higher rate of off ending compared with peers without learning disability (and peers with a more severe learning disability, who rarely commit off ences). In a Swedish birth cohort study, Hodgins (1992) found that 'intellectually handicapped' men were three times more likely to off end than men with no disorder or handicap, andfi ve times more likely to commit a violent off ence. Women with intellectual handicap were almost four times more likely to off end and 25 times more likely to commit a violent off ence than the control group. (Retrieved from http://apt.rcpsych.org/content/aptrcpsych/6/4/278.full.pdf)

stem: When asked how many legs a dog has, a 26-year-old male prisoner answers 'fi ve legs'. This is known as
explanation: This is called Ganser's Syndrome. It is often termed as a factitious disorder though ICD-10 considers it as a dissociative state.

stem: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis in adolescents with a history of self-harm?
explanation: The prevalence of self-harm among children and adolescents with mental health issues was about 1%. There is a very strong association with depression and suicidality in young people. "Instances of self-harm in adolescence are frequently associated with feelings or symptoms of depression, including clinical depression, as well as personality disturbance or disorder. Experiencing a mental health problem is a risk factor for both self-harm and suicide. Evidence suggests that more than 90% of people who present to hospital with self-harm have a mental disorder, the most common being depression. A history of mental illness, in particular, depression, as well as the presence of more than one mental disorder is a strong predictor of suicide". (Excerpt retrieved from Ref: Skegg K. Self-harm. stem: Which of the followingfi ndings is most commonly seen in anorexia nervosa?
explanation: Raised serum urea and creatinine is seen in anorexia due to dehydration. There is often a minimal elevation of LFTs while lipids may be dramatically elevated due to starvation. Electrolyte disturbances are varied in form and are often present in those who vomit frequently or misuse large quantities of laxatives or diuretics. Vomiting results in metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia; laxative misuse results in metabolic acidosis, hyponatraemia and hypokalemia. Hypophosphataemia and hypomagnesemia are also seen in anorexia patients. Hypophosphataemia could be exaggerated during re-feeding.

stem: What medication would you NOT prescribe to a child with ADHD and hepatic impairment?
explanation: The MHRA committee on safety of medicines (CSM) issued a warning in January 2005 about "the risk of rare (estimated incidence less than 1 in 50,000 patients) but sometimes severe hepatic disorders linked with atomoxetine. Atomoxetine should be discontinued in patients with jaundice or laboratory evidence of liver injury, and should not be started on those who have an established impairment".

stem: Teratogenicity (1) Your consultant has a list of 4 patients who are pregnant and on various psychotropic medications. All of them had a detailed ultrasonography at 16-18 weeks. correctAnswer: Lamotrigine → Facial clefts, Diazepam → Facial clefts, Carbamazepine → Neural tube defects, Sodium valproate → Neural tube defects 
explanation: Explanation: Diazepam is a longer acting benzodiazepine. There is an association between benzodiazepines (diazepam) and increased risk of facial clefts and, therefore, detailed ultrasonography at 16-18 weeks is indicated. Carbamazepine is associated with neural tube defects (hence folic acid supplementation is recommended for women of child-bearing age). Sodium valproate is associated with neural tube defects (Therefore folic acid supplementation is recommended for women of child-bearing age). Valproate has also been associated with increased risk of hypospadias. Detailed ultrasonography at 16-18 weeks is indicated, and maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein levels should be measured if patients are either on carbamazepine or sodium valproate. Data for Lamotrigine suggest a low risk of fetal malformations when used as monotherapy although a substantially increased risk of cleft palate has been reported. Lamotrigine monotherapy is associated with a 3.2% frequency of malformations.
